title: Strategies to help students experience success
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino, a secondary science teacher, shares five classroom strategies for helping students, especially those with weak schemas, limited working memory or low habits of challenge, experience success. Each strategy is given a why and a how. They are: provide a booklet students can refer to, build in retrieval of past content, make expectations for answer phrasing explicit through modelling and choral response, give a lot of sentence-level writing practice, and have students answer many carefully sequenced questions. She cites Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, Adam Boxer's retrieval roulette, Because-But-So, and guidance fading. The honest caveats are that choral response is new to her and unmeasured. The through-line is that explicit support up front prevents the reactive rescuing she used to do, and small successes create confidence for bigger challenges.
points: A well-designed topic booklet gives every student access to the content, including those who missed a lesson.
Retrieval should be built into lessons, with simple warm-up questions or keyword recall to reassure classes that they can do the work.
Modelling answers and choral response teach students exactly how to phrase science answers so they can join discussion.
Sentence-level writing practice such as Because, But, So works best after knowledge is secure and with worked and faded examples.
Sequencing of practice questions matters more than their number, and controlled sequencing is reinforced with verbal questioning.
quotes: As a teacher, however, I have come to focus on the second part more and I think that is our job in a nutshell. We are changing the things that we can through instructing, modelling and supporting our students, continually adapting to our classes.

Why: Students will struggle to achieve any success if they don’t have the material to access when answering questions about a topic. We cannot expect them to simply guess what we have in our heads, especially if they have missed a lesson for any reason.

Ebbinghaus’ forgetting curve is famous as it gives us a template of forgetting that we can work with when teaching and encouraging retrieval. When students first learn something, the retention rate is very high but over time, this drops.

My previous style of teaching would include teaching them a concept followed by a worksheet with questions where they applied their new learning. I always had some students in every class who simply could not access the questions and if they did attempt them, would use keywords incorrectly or miss out important detail. I would go and support them but this is a reactive response to something that I could have avoided from the start.

This is something I resisted for a very long time despite reading about its benefits in the classroom. I was worried my older GCSE students would laugh at the thought of doing it. Nonetheless, I trialled it with my classes and found it oddly reassuring.

The biggest hurdle is a lack of prerequisite knowledge but sometimes this could be all we focus on and students miss out on actually writing well reasoned and detailed responses. The best way to get students to achieve good writing is by getting them to practice good writing.

Ultimately, we want to develop confident learners so they can attempt challenging questions and make important connections between concepts. But the first step? Provide students with chances to experience small successes so they can move on to bigger ones.
